title: Rebel verbs
goal: Master the past tense of irregular verbs — a small group that happens to be the most used — through a story that contains them all.
bekal: recognize and use thirty irregular past forms
see the pattern: many change their vowel in groups
tell about past events without stumbling
wave: Review **unit 16** first: name five things you like and five you don't, out loud, with *kan godt lide* and *kan ikke lide*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Historien om en tabt cykel
dialogs.intro: Budi tells Mette and Ahmad what happened on Saturday. Almost every verb is irregular — watch for them.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: I lørdags gik jeg til byen for at købe en bog.
lines.id: Last Saturday I walked into town to buy a book.
lines.literal: last-Saturday went I to town-the for to buy a book.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Gik du? Du har jo en cykel.
lines.id: You walked? You have a bike, don't you?
lines.literal: went you? you have after-all a bike.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det er pointen. Jeg tog cyklen, men jeg fandt den ikke bagefter.
lines.id: That's the point. I took the bike, but I couldn't find it afterwards.
lines.literal: it is point-the. I took bike-the, but I found it not afterwards.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det var problemet. Jeg vidste det ikke. Der stod tres cykler.
lines.id: That was the problem. I didn't know. There were sixty bikes there.
lines.literal: it was problem-the. I knew it not. there stood sixty bikes.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.id: Did you look for the lock?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja. Jeg gik rundt i en halv time. Så fik jeg en idé.
lines.id: Yes. I walked around for half an hour. Then I had an idea.
lines.literal: yes. I went round in a half hour. then got I an idea.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg gav min nøgle til en tilfældig cykel. Den passede.
lines.id: I tried my key on a random bike. It fit.
lines.literal: I gave my key to a random bike. it fitted.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nej. Jeg sad på en fremmed cykel i ti minutter, før jeg forstod det.
lines.id: No. I sat on a stranger's bike for ten minutes before I realized.
lines.literal: no. I sat on a strange bike in ten minutes, before I understood it.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.id: And what did the owner say?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Han lo. Og så hjalp han mig med at finde min egen.
lines.id: He laughed. And then he helped me find my own.
lines.literal: he laughed. and then helped he me with to find my own.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Meget dansk. Vi griner, og bagefter hjælper vi.
lines.id: Very Danish. We laugh, and then we help.
lines.literal: very Danish. we laugh, and afterwards help we.

notes: **Count the past forms.** This dialog contains fifteen irregular verbs: *gik*, *tog*, *fandt*, *satte*, *var*, *vidste*, *stod*, *så*, *fik*, *gav*, *sad*, *forstod*, *sagde*, *lo*, *hjalp*. Reread it and mark them — that's more useful practice than memorizing a table.
**For at** = "in order to". *Jeg gik til byen **for at** købe en bog.* This is the standard way to express purpose, and it needs both words: *for* alone isn't enough.

**Du har jo en cykel** — *jo* in mid-sentence is different from the answer *jo* in unit 10. Here it means "you know", "after all", pointing to something you both already know. One of the typical Danish softening words.

**Så du efter…?** — *at se efter* = to look for, to check. Also notice that the past of *at se* is **så**, spelled exactly like *så* meaning "then". Danish is full of twins like this; context sorts them out.
**Sagde** is pronounced **SAH-uh** — the *g* and *d* aren't heard at all. One of the biggest gaps between spelling and sound in Danish, and it happens in one of the most common words.
**Lo** is the past of *at le* (to laugh) — two letters, one of the shortest forms in Danish. There's also *at grine*, which is regular (*grinede*) and more everyday.

grammars.title: Thirty irregular past forms
body: This list is short, and that's the good news. The bad news: every word on it is one you use every day, so none can be skipped.
The last form column is included now on purpose — the "have done" form from unit 19. Learning all three at once costs far less than learning them twice.
after: ⚠️ *Sagde* = **SAH-uh**, *havde* = **HAH-dhuh**, *gjorde* = **GYOH-ah**. Three words that sound far from how they're written, and all three are among the ten most used verbs.
Notice that *er gået*, *er kommet*, *er blevet*, *er løbet* use **er**, not *har*. These are verbs of movement or change of state; the full rule is in unit 19.

grammars.title: The pattern isn't as random as it looks
body: Memorizing thirty words one by one is tiring. Learning them in groups that rhyme is much cheaper — and these groups are real, inherited from the same old Germanic language that gave English *sing-sang-sung*.
after: As an English speaker, the last column is savings you didn't know you had. Danish and English share ancestors, and the irregular verbs are exactly where that heritage survives most faithfully.

blocks.text: These sentences contain the most common irregular verbs and are ready to use right away.
*Det gjorde ondt* = that hurt (physically). *At gøre ondt* is used for pain: *Min ryg gør ondt* = my back hurts. For "hurt" in the sense of sad: *det var trist*.

sections.title: A story to read out loud

blocks.text: Read this paragraph out loud twice. First for the sound, then marking every past form you recognize.

*I sidste uge **var** jeg i Aarhus. Jeg **tog** toget om morgenen og **kom** frem klokken ti. Vejret **var** dejligt, så jeg **gik** en lang tur langs havnen. Jeg **så** museet, men jeg **gik** ikke ind — der **stod** en meget lang kø. I stedet **fandt** jeg en lille café, hvor jeg **drak** kaffe og **skrev** postkort. Om eftermiddagen **besøgte** jeg en gammel ven. Vi **snakkede** i tre timer, og han **fortalte** om sit nye arbejde. Han **spurgte**, om jeg **ville** blive til aftensmad, men jeg **sagde** nej — jeg **skulle** nå toget klokken syv. Til sidst **gav** han mig en pose kage med hjem. Det **var** en god dag.*

blocks.title: Three ways to use the paragraph above
items: **Translate it into English** without a dictionary. Whatever you don't understand is your next study list.
**Rewrite it in the present tense.** *Jeg er i Aarhus. Jeg tager toget…* This makes you recognize the verb pairs from both directions.
**Write your own version** with the same structure, about a trip you've taken. The frame is already there; you just swap the content.
We took the train to Aarhus.

exercises.prompt: Change these sentences to the past tense.
Put the words in the right order.
items: byen / gik / jeg / til / lørdags / i

answers: var — havde — gik — så — fik — sagde — tog — vidste
I går så jeg en film. — Jeg vidste det ikke. — Vi tog toget til Aarhus. — Han hjalp mig meget. — Jeg fik en god idé. — Hvad sagde ejeren?
Jeg gik til byen. — Hun tog toget. — Vi så en film. — Han sagde ingenting. — De hjalp mig.
I lørdags gik jeg til byen. — Jeg vidste det ikke. — Jeg fik en god idé. — Han lo. — Han hjalp mig meget.
